title: A Collapsing Star Produced an Afterglow Brighter Than Its Galaxy - Nautilus
gist: Paywall-truncated report on a gamma-ray burst seen by NASA's Fermi Gamma Ray Space Telescope. The gamma-ray emission was modest, but the afterglow was among the brightest 1% of observed events and outshone its host galaxy, with roughly a billion years of the Sun's energy output packed into a narrow beam.

insights.claim: NASA's Fermi Gamma Ray Space Telescope, in low Earth orbit, detected one of the brightest bursts of light in decades: an intense afterglow after a gamma-ray burst from a collapsing star.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Shows the scientific return from space-based observatories, relevant to the space science budget debate.
insights.quote: one of the brightest bursts of light in decades

insights.claim: The burst's gamma-ray light was modest, but its afterglow was among the brightest 1 percent of observed events in a newly published comparison study.

insights.so_what: A burst's brightness at one wavelength does not predict its afterglow, which matters for how such events are classified.
